lessons.title: Inspect command help
lessons.about: Get-Help explains cmdlets, concepts, syntax, parameters, and examples without leaving the PowerShell session.
breakdown: The command name selects the help topic.
-Parameter narrows the page to one parameter.
lessons.task: Print the name of Get-ChildItem's Path parameter from local help.
hints: Select the Name property from the parameter help object.

checks.description: The Path parameter name was printed.

lessons.completion: Help is discoverable from the shell; add -Examples or -Full when you need more context.

lessons.title: Discover available commands
lessons.about: Get-Command searches cmdlets, functions, aliases, scripts, and applications available in the current session.
lessons.example_output:
CommandType Name        Version Source
----------- ----        ------- ------
Cmdlet      Get-Content 3.1.0.0 Microsoft.PowerShell.Management
breakdown: A precise name returns one command definition.
CommandType distinguishes cmdlets from aliases and applications.
lessons.task: Print only the command type of Get-ChildItem.
hints: Expand the CommandType property.

checks.description: Get-ChildItem was identified as a cmdlet.

lessons.completion: Get-Command is the quickest inventory of what PowerShell can run.

lessons.title: Resolve aliases
lessons.about: Get-Alias shows which full PowerShell command an abbreviated alias resolves to, making unfamiliar commands easier to read.
lessons.example_output:
CommandType Name Version Source
----------- ---- ------- ------
Alias       ls -> Get-ChildItem
breakdown: ls is an alias in Windows PowerShell.
Definition contains the full target command.
lessons.task: Print the full command behind the dir alias.
hints: Expand the Definition property.

checks.description: The alias resolved to Get-ChildItem.

lessons.completion: Aliases are convenient interactively; full cmdlet names are clearer in scripts.

lessons.title: Show the current location
lessons.about: Get-Location returns a PathInfo object for the current location instead of printing an unstructured path string.
breakdown: The current provider exposes a location.
The Path property contains its text representation.
lessons.task: Print only the absolute path of the disposable practice directory.
hints: Expand the Path property from Get-Location.

checks.description: The current practice path was printed.

lessons.completion: PowerShell locations can represent file-system paths and other providers.

lessons.title: Change the current location
lessons.about: Set-Location changes the active location for the current PowerShell process, affecting later relative paths.
breakdown: The relative path is resolved below the current directory.
A successful location change normally emits no output.
lessons.task: Change into the existing reports directory and print its leaf name.
hints: Pass the directory name as the path.

checks.description: The active location is the reports directory.

lessons.completion: Set-Location changes only this disposable PowerShell process.

lessons.title: List child items
lessons.about: Get-ChildItem enumerates files, directories, registry keys, variables, and other provider-backed collections.
breakdown: Without a path, the current location is listed.
-Name returns compact names instead of FileInfo objects.
lessons.task: Print only the names of the two files in the practice directory.
hints: Combine the switches that select files and request names only.

checks.description: Both file names and no extras were printed.

lessons.completion: Get-ChildItem is PowerShell's general collection enumerator.

lessons.title: Inspect one item
lessons.about: Get-Item retrieves the object representing one path so its metadata can flow through the object pipeline.
breakdown: The path resolves one FileInfo object.
Length measures the file in bytes.
lessons.task: Print only the byte length of note.txt.
hints: Expand the Length property.

checks.description: The six-byte file length was printed.

lessons.completion: Get-Item retrieves an object; Get-ChildItem enumerates a collection.

lessons.title: Test whether a path exists
lessons.about: Test-Path returns a Boolean and can distinguish leaves such as files from containers such as directories.
breakdown: The path is checked without opening it.
-PathType Leaf requires a non-container item.
lessons.task: Confirm that config.json exists and is a file.
hints: Use -PathType Leaf.

checks.description: The path test returned True.

lessons.completion: Test-Path is useful for defensive scripts before reading, moving, or deleting paths.

lessons.title: Resolve an absolute path
lessons.about: Resolve-Path converts an existing relative or wildcard path into resolved provider path objects.
breakdown: The input path must already exist.
The Path property contains the resolved absolute path.
lessons.task: Print only the absolute path to note.txt.
hints: Expand the Path property.

checks.description: The resolved file path was printed.

lessons.completion: Resolve-Path is valuable before logging or validating the exact path a script will use.

lessons.title: Combine path segments
lessons.about: Join-Path combines parent and child segments with the separator rules of the active PowerShell provider.
breakdown: The first argument is the parent path.
The second argument is the child segment.
lessons.task: Combine reports and daily.txt into one relative Windows path.
hints: Pass the parent first and child second.

checks.description: The Windows path segments were joined.

lessons.completion: Join-Path avoids hard-coding path separators in scripts.

lessons.title: Create a new item
lessons.about: New-Item creates files, directories, and items exposed by other providers using an explicit item type.
lessons.example_output:
Directory: C:\work
Mode LastWriteTime Length Name
---- ------------- ------ ----
d---- ...                 reports
breakdown: -ItemType Directory requests a container.
-Path names the new directory.
lessons.task: Create a directory named reports and print its name.
hints: Create a Directory, then expand Name.

checks.description: The reports directory exists.
The new directory name was printed.

lessons.completion: New-Item works consistently across providers; the item type controls what is created.

lessons.title: Copy a file
lessons.about: Copy-Item duplicates file-system items while leaving the source in place.
breakdown: The first path is the source.
The second path is the destination.
lessons.task: Copy source.txt to backup.txt without changing the source.
hints: Pass source and destination in that order.

checks.description: The backup contains the source text.
The source remains unchanged.

lessons.completion: Copy-Item is silent on success unless -PassThru is requested.

lessons.title: Move a file
lessons.about: Move-Item relocates an item and can give it a different destination name in one operation.
breakdown: The source is removed from its original path.
The destination may be a new relative path.
lessons.task: Move draft.txt to archive\final.txt.
hints: Use the complete destination path.

checks.description: The moved file has the original content.
The original draft path is gone.

lessons.completion: Move-Item changes location; Copy-Item deliberately keeps the source.

lessons.title: Rename an item
lessons.about: Rename-Item changes an item's name while keeping it in the same parent location.
breakdown: The existing item comes first.
-NewName may also be used for clarity.
lessons.task: Rename report.draft to report.final.
hints: Provide the old and new names.

checks.description: The final report exists with its content.
The draft name is gone.

lessons.completion: Rename-Item does not move an item to a different parent directory.

lessons.title: Remove a disposable item
lessons.about: Remove-Item deletes provider items; this rep confines it to one synthetic file in the temporary workspace.
breakdown: The relative path stays inside the current workspace.
Successful deletion is normally silent.
lessons.task: Delete the disposable file named trash.txt.
hints: Pass the file path directly.

checks.description: The disposable file was removed.

lessons.completion: Use -WhatIf with Remove-Item outside a disposable workspace when reviewing a broad deletion.

lessons.title: Read file content
lessons.about: Get-Content reads a text file as objects, usually emitting one string object per line.
breakdown: Each line enters the success pipeline separately.
-Raw can instead return one multiline string.
lessons.task: Print all three lines from briefing.txt.
hints: Pass the file name to Get-Content.

checks.description: All briefing lines were printed in order.

lessons.completion: Get-Content produces pipeline objects, making each line easy to filter or transform.

lessons.title: Replace file content
lessons.about: Set-Content writes new values to a file, replacing the previous contents rather than appending.
breakdown: -Path selects the destination file.
-Value supplies the replacement content.
lessons.task: Replace status.txt so it contains only ready.
hints: Use -Value to replace the old text.

checks.description: The status file contains only ready.

lessons.completion: Set-Content replaces; Add-Content appends. Choose intentionally.

lessons.title: Append file content
lessons.about: Add-Content adds values after existing file content without replacing what is already there.
breakdown: The destination already exists.
The new value is appended as another line.
lessons.task: Append beta to log.txt after its existing alpha line.
hints: Use Add-Content with the existing path.

checks.description: Both log lines are present in order.

lessons.completion: Add-Content is appropriate for simple append-only output such as practice logs.

lessons.title: Empty a file without deleting it
lessons.about: Clear-Content removes a file's text while preserving the file item itself.
breakdown: The path continues to exist.
Only the stored content is cleared.
lessons.task: Empty cache.txt but keep the file.
hints: Clear the content rather than removing the item.

checks.description: The cache file still exists.
The cache file is empty.

lessons.completion: Clear-Content preserves the file path and metadata while removing its stored text.

lessons.title: Calculate a file digest
lessons.about: Get-FileHash computes a cryptographic digest and returns an object containing the algorithm, hash, and path.
breakdown: SHA256 selects a common digest algorithm.
The Hash property is a 64-character hexadecimal string.
lessons.task: Print only the SHA-256 hash of artifact.txt.
hints: Expand the Hash property.

checks.description: A 64-character SHA-256 digest was printed.

lessons.completion: A digest verifies exact bytes only when you also trust the expected digest.

lessons.title: Search text with patterns
lessons.about: Select-String searches strings and files with regular expressions and returns rich MatchInfo objects.
breakdown: -Path selects the file to search.
-Pattern accepts a regular expression.
lessons.task: Print only the matching ERROR line from service.log.
hints: Expand the Line property from MatchInfo.

files.service.log:
INFO started
ERROR connection failed
INFO retrying

checks.description: Only the error line was printed.

lessons.completion: Select-String preserves match metadata such as file, line number, and captured matches.

lessons.title: Measure pipeline objects
lessons.about: Measure-Object counts objects and can calculate numeric sums, averages, minima, maxima, words, lines, and characters.
breakdown: Get-Content emits line objects.
-Line requests a line-oriented measurement.
lessons.task: Print only the number of lines in events.txt.
hints: Expand the Lines property.

checks.description: The three-line count was printed.

lessons.completion: Measure-Object works on pipeline objects rather than parsing a display table.

lessons.title: Sort objects
lessons.about: Sort-Object orders objects by values or named properties and can remove duplicates with -Unique.
breakdown: String objects are sorted by value.
Object collections can instead be sorted by property.
lessons.task: Print the host names in alphabetical order.
hints: Pipe the lines into Sort-Object.

checks.description: The hosts were sorted alphabetically.

lessons.completion: Sort-Object understands properties, so structured objects rarely need text parsing first.

lessons.title: Group objects by property
lessons.about: Group-Object collects objects that share a property value and exposes each group's name, count, and members.
breakdown: status is read as an object property.
Each result represents one distinct property value.
lessons.task: Group inventory.csv by status, sort group names, and print only each count.
lessons.solution: Import-Csv inventory.csv | Group-Object status | Sort-Object Name | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Count
hints: Group on status, sort on Name, then expand Count.

checks.description: The active and idle group counts were printed.

lessons.completion: Group-Object replaces many manual counting loops with structured grouping.

lessons.title: Choose properties or objects
lessons.about: Select-Object projects properties, limits collections, and expands a property into its raw values.
breakdown: -First limits the collection.
-Property chooses the output shape.
lessons.task: Print only the name value from every record in people.csv.
hints: Use -ExpandProperty rather than -Property.

checks.description: Both names were printed as plain values.

lessons.completion: -Property keeps objects; -ExpandProperty emits the selected property's values.

lessons.title: Filter objects by property
lessons.about: Where-Object filters pipeline objects using property comparison syntax or a script block.
lessons.example_output:
name status
---- ------
web  active
db   active
breakdown: status identifies the property.
-eq active keeps matching objects.
lessons.task: Print the names of only active inventory records.
lessons.solution: Import-Csv inventory.csv | Where-Object status -eq active | Select-Object -ExpandProperty name
hints: Use the property comparison form, then expand name.

checks.description: Only active item names were printed.

lessons.completion: Filter objects before formatting so downstream commands retain their properties.

lessons.title: Transform every pipeline value
lessons.about: ForEach-Object invokes a safe member or processing expression once for each incoming pipeline object.
breakdown: Each line is a System.String object.
-MemberName invokes the ToUpper method on each string.
lessons.task: Convert every line in words.txt to uppercase.
hints: Use -MemberName ToUpper.

checks.description: Every word was converted to uppercase.

lessons.completion: PowerShell passes string objects here, so their methods are available directly.

lessons.title: Remove adjacent duplicate values
lessons.about: Get-Unique removes adjacent duplicates, so sorting first is the reliable way to deduplicate an unordered list.
breakdown: Sort-Object places equal values together.
Get-Unique keeps one object from each adjacent run.
lessons.task: Print the unique colors in alphabetical order.
hints: Sort before Get-Unique.

checks.description: Unique colors were printed in order.

lessons.completion: For property-based deduplication, Sort-Object -Unique is often more direct.

lessons.title: Compare two object collections
lessons.about: Compare-Object reports values present only in a reference collection or only in a difference collection.
breakdown: Reference-only values use <=.
Difference-only values use =>.
lessons.task: Compare the inline sets and print only the differing values.
hints: Expand InputObject from the comparison results.

checks.description: The two differing values were printed.

lessons.completion: SideIndicator explains which collection contains each unmatched object.

lessons.title: Save and continue a pipeline
lessons.about: Tee-Object sends pipeline input to a file or variable while also passing the same objects downstream.
breakdown: -FilePath stores the pipeline values.
The same values remain visible on stdout.
lessons.task: Print source.txt while saving the same lines to copy.txt.
hints: Use -FilePath for the side copy.

checks.description: The original lines continued through the pipeline.
The tee file contains the same lines.

lessons.completion: Tee-Object is useful for capturing intermediate pipeline data without stopping the flow.

lessons.title: Parse CSV text into objects
lessons.about: ConvertFrom-Csv turns comma-separated text already in the pipeline into objects whose headers become properties.
breakdown: The first input line supplies property names.
Later rows become custom objects.
lessons.task: Parse records.csv and print only the role value.
hints: Convert the lines, then expand role.

checks.description: The parsed role property was printed.

lessons.completion: Use ConvertFrom-Csv for CSV text already in memory; Import-Csv reads a file directly.

lessons.title: Serialize objects as CSV text
lessons.about: ConvertTo-Csv converts object properties into CSV-formatted string lines without writing a file.
breakdown: Object property names become the header.
-NoTypeInformation omits the legacy type metadata line.
lessons.task: Convert people.csv back into CSV text without type information.
hints: Use -NoTypeInformation for clean CSV.

checks.description: The CSV text contains Alice's record.
The CSV header was emitted.

lessons.completion: ConvertTo-Csv returns strings; Export-Csv writes them to a file.

lessons.title: Import a CSV file as objects
lessons.about: Import-Csv reads a delimited file and creates one object per row using the header fields as properties.
lessons.example_output:
name  team
----  ----
alice blue
bob   red
breakdown: The header defines name and team properties.
Each data row becomes one object.
lessons.task: Import people.csv and print only each team value.
hints: Expand the team property.

checks.description: Both team values were printed.

lessons.completion: Imported rows are objects, so sorting and filtering can address properties by name.

lessons.title: Export objects to a CSV file
lessons.about: Export-Csv writes object properties to a reusable comma-separated file.
breakdown: Pipeline objects supply the rows.
The output path receives a new CSV file.
lessons.task: Export only the blue-team records from people.csv to blue.csv.
lessons.solution: Import-Csv people.csv | Where-Object team -eq blue | Export-Csv blue.csv -NoTypeInformation
hints: Filter before Export-Csv.

checks.description: The exported CSV contains only Alice's blue-team row.

lessons.completion: Export-Csv serializes visible object properties, so select the intended shape first.

lessons.title: Serialize objects as JSON
lessons.about: ConvertTo-Json serializes PowerShell objects into JSON for APIs, configuration, logs, and interchange.
breakdown: Properties become JSON keys.
-Compress removes indentation and extra whitespace.
lessons.task: Convert the single object in person.csv to compact JSON.
hints: Use -Compress for one line.

checks.description: The compact JSON object was printed.

lessons.completion: JSON preserves structured property names instead of relying on display formatting.

lessons.title: Parse JSON into objects
lessons.about: ConvertFrom-Json turns JSON text into PowerShell objects whose properties can be selected, filtered, and transformed.
breakdown: -Raw keeps the JSON document as one string.
JSON keys become PowerShell properties.
lessons.task: Parse person.json and print only the name property.
hints: Read with -Raw, convert, then expand name.

checks.description: The parsed name was printed.

lessons.completion: ConvertFrom-Json makes JSON properties available to the object pipeline.

lessons.title: Serialize objects as XML
lessons.about: ConvertTo-Xml represents PowerShell objects and their properties in an XML document or string.
breakdown: -As String returns XML text.
-NoTypeInformation keeps the document focused on properties.
lessons.task: Convert person.csv to XML text without type information.
hints: Use -As String and -NoTypeInformation.

checks.description: The XML contains an Objects root.
The XML contains Alice's value.

lessons.completion: ConvertTo-Xml is useful when XML consumers need an object's property data.

lessons.title: Query XML with XPath
lessons.about: Select-Xml applies an XPath expression to XML files or nodes and returns match objects.
breakdown: -Path supplies the XML document.
-XPath selects matching nodes anywhere below the root.
lessons.task: Query config.xml and print the port node's inner text.
lessons.solution: Select-Xml -Path config.xml -XPath '//port' | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Node | Select-Object -ExpandProperty InnerText
hints: Expand Node, then InnerText.

checks.description: The XML port value was printed.

lessons.completion: XPath is precise for structured XML and avoids brittle string matching.

lessons.title: Render objects as HTML
lessons.about: ConvertTo-Html builds an HTML table or list from the properties of pipeline objects.
breakdown: Imported objects provide columns and rows.
-Fragment omits the outer html and body document tags.
lessons.task: Convert people.csv to an HTML table fragment.
hints: Use -Fragment and collect the lines with Out-String.

checks.description: An HTML table was produced.
The table contains Alice's row.

lessons.completion: Select the intended properties before ConvertTo-Html to control table columns.

lessons.title: Write display output to a file
lessons.about: Out-File sends formatted pipeline output to a text file with an explicit encoding.
breakdown: Pipeline text becomes file content.
An explicit encoding makes later reads predictable.
lessons.task: Write the word ready to status.txt using ASCII encoding.
hints: Pipe Write-Output into Out-File and set -Encoding ascii.

checks.description: The output file contains ready.

lessons.completion: Out-File writes formatted text; Export-Csv and ConvertTo-Json preserve more structure.

lessons.title: Inspect a variable
lessons.about: Get-Variable returns variable metadata or, with -ValueOnly, the value stored in a named PowerShell variable.
breakdown: PWD names the current-location variable without a dollar sign.
-ValueOnly emits its PathInfo value.
lessons.task: Read PWD and print only its Path property for this disposable rep.
hints: Use PWD without $, then expand the Path property.

checks.description: The disposable workspace path was printed.

lessons.completion: Get-Variable can inspect scope, options, descriptions, and values without dynamic evaluation.

lessons.title: Create or update a variable
lessons.about: Set-Variable creates or changes a named variable and can return the resulting variable object with -PassThru.
breakdown: -Name omits the dollar-sign syntax.
-PassThru makes the otherwise silent change observable.
lessons.task: Set Mode to practice and print only the stored value.
hints: Request -PassThru, then expand Value.

checks.description: The new variable value was printed.

lessons.completion: Variables created here disappear with the disposable PowerShell process.

lessons.title: Remove a variable
lessons.about: Remove-Variable deletes a variable from the selected scope without treating its name as executable code.
breakdown: The variable name is supplied without $.
Successful removal normally emits no output.
lessons.task: Create Mode, remove it, then prove Variable:Mode no longer exists.
lessons.solution: Set-Variable Mode practice; Remove-Variable Mode; Test-Path Variable:Mode
hints: Use Test-Path against the Variable provider after removal.

checks.description: The removed variable no longer exists.

lessons.completion: Variable changes remain inside this one disposable PowerShell process.

lessons.title: Inspect object properties and methods
lessons.about: Get-Member reveals the type, properties, methods, events, and adapted members available on pipeline objects.
breakdown: The incoming FileInfo determines the member list.
-Name can narrow the inspection.
lessons.task: Confirm that note.txt's object exposes a member named Length.
lessons.solution: Get-Item note.txt | Get-Member -Name Length | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Name
hints: Filter Get-Member with -Name Length.

checks.description: The Length member name was printed.

lessons.completion: Get-Member is the bridge from seeing output to understanding usable object data.

lessons.title: Write to the success pipeline
lessons.about: Write-Output sends objects to PowerShell's success stream so later pipeline stages can process them.
breakdown: Each argument becomes a pipeline object.
The host renders objects only at the pipeline's end.
lessons.task: Write alpha, beta, and gamma as three pipeline values.
hints: Pass the three values as arguments.

checks.description: All three values were emitted in order.

lessons.completion: Write-Output participates in the pipeline; Write-Host is presentation-oriented.

lessons.title: Write presentation text
lessons.about: Write-Host writes display-oriented information for a person at the console rather than data intended for processing.
breakdown: The quoted text is one argument.
Host output is intended for presentation.
lessons.task: Display the exact phrase practice ready.
hints: Quote the two-word phrase.

checks.description: The presentation text was displayed.

lessons.completion: Prefer Write-Output for reusable data and Write-Host for intentional human-facing display.

lessons.title: Format objects as a table
lessons.about: Format-Table creates display instructions that arrange selected properties into columns for terminal reading.
breakdown: The property list defines columns.
Formatting belongs at the end of a data pipeline.
lessons.task: Display name and team from people.csv as a table without headers.
hints: Use -HideTableHeaders, then Out-String.

checks.description: The table contains Alice.
The table contains the blue team.

lessons.completion: After Format-Table, the pipeline contains formatting data rather than the original objects.

lessons.title: Format properties vertically
lessons.about: Format-List displays one property per line, which is useful when an object has more properties than fit in a table.
breakdown: The property list controls what is shown.
Each property appears on its own line.
lessons.task: Display the name and level properties from person.csv as a list.
hints: Format the two properties, then collect the display text.

checks.description: The list contains the name value.
The list contains the level value.

lessons.completion: Format-List is for presentation; select properties before formatting when data continues downstream.

lessons.title: Convert display output to strings
lessons.about: Out-String converts pipeline output into rendered text and can emit one string per input line with -Stream.
breakdown: Get-Content supplies a string object.
-Stream avoids combining everything into one multiline string.
lessons.task: Render note.txt through Out-String in streaming mode.
hints: Use the -Stream switch.

checks.description: The rendered note text was printed.

lessons.completion: Out-String is useful at the boundary where structured output must become display text.

lessons.title: Emit a warning stream message
lessons.about: Write-Warning sends a non-terminating advisory message to PowerShell's warning stream without treating it as success data.
breakdown: The message is tagged as a warning.
Warnings can be handled separately from normal output.
lessons.task: Emit a warning containing the phrase check configuration.
hints: Pass the phrase as one quoted warning message.

checks.description: The warning message was emitted.
The warning did not fail the command.

lessons.completion: Warnings communicate concern without automatically terminating a script.

lessons.title: Separate path components
lessons.about: Split-Path extracts parent paths, leaf names, qualifiers, and other components without manual string splitting.
breakdown: The input is a relative Windows path.
-Parent returns everything above the leaf name.
lessons.task: Print the parent portion of reports\daily.txt.
hints: Request the -Parent component.

checks.description: The parent path was printed.

lessons.completion: Split-Path understands provider syntax and is safer than splitting on backslashes.

lessons.title: Convert to a provider-native path
lessons.about: Convert-Path converts an existing PowerShell provider path into its native path representation.
breakdown: The input item must exist.
The result is a plain native path string.
lessons.task: Print the native absolute path to note.txt.
hints: Pass the existing relative file path.

checks.description: The native file path was printed.

lessons.completion: Resolve-Path returns PathInfo objects; Convert-Path returns native path strings.

lessons.title: List PowerShell drives
lessons.about: Get-PSDrive lists logical drives exposed by providers, including file systems, variables, functions, aliases, and the registry.
lessons.example_output:
Name Used (GB) Free (GB) Provider   Root
---- --------- --------- --------   ----
C                        FileSystem C:\
breakdown: -PSProvider filters by provider type.
File-system drive names can be used like normal PowerShell locations.
lessons.task: Print the name of the first file-system PowerShell drive.
hints: Filter to FileSystem and select the first Name.

checks.description: A file-system drive name was printed.

lessons.completion: PowerShell drives provide a consistent navigation model across different data stores.

lessons.title: Inspect available providers
lessons.about: Get-PSProvider lists the engines that expose data stores through PowerShell's drive and path model.
breakdown: Providers define path semantics and capabilities.
Each provider can expose one or more PowerShell drives.
lessons.task: Print the names of all providers available in this Windows PowerShell session.
hints: Expand the Name property.

checks.description: The FileSystem provider was listed.
The Registry provider was listed.

lessons.completion: Providers explain why familiar cmdlets can work with more than files.

lessons.title: Read item properties
lessons.about: Get-ItemProperty retrieves properties stored on provider items and returns them as PowerShell object properties.
breakdown: The file-system provider returns FileInfo-like metadata.
Select-Object can isolate one property value.
lessons.task: Print only the byte length property of note.txt.
hints: Expand the Length property.

checks.description: The six-byte length was printed.

lessons.completion: Get-ItemProperty reads provider metadata without parsing formatted listings.

lessons.title: Create a ZIP archive
lessons.about: Compress-Archive packages files and directories into a standard ZIP archive without an external utility.
breakdown: -Path selects the source directory.
-DestinationPath names the ZIP file.
lessons.task: Create evidence.zip from the evidence directory.
hints: Provide both source and destination paths.

checks.description: The ZIP archive was created.

lessons.completion: Compress-Archive creates ZIP files; verify the source selection before archiving sensitive data.

lessons.title: Extract a ZIP archive
lessons.about: Expand-Archive extracts ZIP contents into a destination directory using native PowerShell cmdlets.
breakdown: The ZIP path is the source.
-DestinationPath controls where contents appear.
lessons.task: Create bundle.zip from note.txt, then extract it into restored.
lessons.solution: Compress-Archive note.txt bundle.zip; Expand-Archive bundle.zip restored
hints: Create the ZIP first, then expand it into restored.

checks.description: The restored file contains the original text.

lessons.completion: Archive extraction stays inside the disposable workspace for this rep.

lessons.title: Serialize objects as CLI XML
lessons.about: Export-Clixml preserves PowerShell object properties and type information in PowerShell's XML serialization format.
breakdown: Pipeline objects supply the serialized records.
The output file is designed for Import-Clixml.
lessons.task: Serialize the objects in people.csv to people.xml.
hints: Import the CSV, then pipe objects to Export-Clixml.

checks.description: The CLI XML file was created.

lessons.completion: CLI XML is PowerShell-specific and retains more object metadata than plain CSV.

lessons.title: Restore serialized PowerShell objects
lessons.about: Import-Clixml reconstructs deserialized PowerShell objects from files created in the CLI XML format.
breakdown: The XML file contains serialized property data.
The restored object exposes its Name property.
lessons.task: Import data.xml and print only its Name property.
hints: Import the file, then expand Name.

checks.description: The restored Name property was printed.

lessons.completion: Imported CLI XML objects are deserialized snapshots rather than live original instances.

lessons.title: Inspect access control information
lessons.about: Get-Acl retrieves the security descriptor and access-control information for a local file or directory.
breakdown: The path stays inside the practice directory.
Owner and Access are structured properties.
lessons.task: Print only the owner recorded on note.txt.
hints: Expand the Owner property.

checks.description: A file owner was printed.

lessons.completion: Get-Acl is read-only; review access rules carefully before applying changes.

lessons.title: Inspect running processes
lessons.about: Get-Process returns live process objects containing identifiers, resource measurements, names, and other metadata.
lessons.example_output:
Handles NPM(K) PM(K) WS(K) CPU(s) Id ProcessName
------- ------ ----- ----- ------ -- -----------
...                         ... 1234 powershell
breakdown: $PID identifies this PowerShell process.
The result is a Process object.
lessons.task: Print only the name of the current PowerShell process.
hints: Query -Id $PID and expand ProcessName.

checks.description: The current process name was printed.

lessons.completion: Get-Process is read-only; process objects can be filtered before any deliberate action.

lessons.title: Preview stopping a process
lessons.about: Stop-Process terminates processes, so this rep requires -WhatIf and only previews the action against its own process.
lessons.example_output: What if: Performing the operation Stop-Process...
breakdown: $PID selects only the current PowerShell process.
-WhatIf prevents the termination.
lessons.task: Preview stopping the current PowerShell process without actually stopping it, then print previewed.
hints: The rep requires the -WhatIf safety switch.

checks.description: The protected preview was confirmed.

lessons.completion: Use -WhatIf to review destructive process selections before acting.

lessons.title: Pause a script briefly
lessons.about: Start-Sleep pauses the current PowerShell process for a specified interval without consuming a busy loop.
breakdown: -Milliseconds accepts short intervals.
A successful pause emits no output.
lessons.task: Pause this disposable process for 10 milliseconds, then print resumed.
hints: Use the -Milliseconds parameter.

checks.description: Execution resumed after the short pause.

lessons.completion: Start-Sleep is useful for polling intervals and controlled retry timing.

lessons.title: Inspect Windows services
lessons.about: Get-Service returns ServiceController objects describing installed Windows services and their current states.
lessons.example_output:
Status Name     DisplayName
------ ----     -----------
Running EventLog Windows Event Log
breakdown: EventLog selects one stable Windows service.
Status and Name remain structured properties.
lessons.task: Print only the service name for Windows Event Log.
hints: Query EventLog and expand Name.

checks.description: The EventLog service name was printed.

lessons.completion: Get-Service is read-only and is the safe first step before any service decision.

lessons.title: Start work in a background job
lessons.about: Start-Job runs a script block in a background PowerShell process and returns a job object that can be inspected, awaited, and cleaned up.
breakdown: The script block contains the background work.
The returned job object tracks state and output.
lessons.task: Start a job that returns ready, wait for it, print state=Completed, and remove the job.
hints: Capture the Start-Job result so the same job can be waited on and removed.

checks.description: The background job reached Completed state.

lessons.completion: Keep the returned job object, retrieve its output, and remove finished jobs so a long session stays tidy.

lessons.title: Inspect a background job
lessons.about: Get-Job returns job objects from the current session, including their identifiers, names, state, and output availability.
breakdown: -Name selects a tracked job without relying on its numeric identifier.
The job remains session-scoped until it is removed.
lessons.task: Start a job named gym-check, wait for it, use Get-Job to print gym-check=Completed, and remove it.
hints: Assign a stable name when starting the job, then query that name after waiting.

checks.description: The named job was found in Completed state.

lessons.completion: Get-Job discovers jobs owned by the current PowerShell session; names make concurrent work easier to identify.

lessons.title: Collect background-job output
lessons.about: Receive-Job transfers available output from a job into the current pipeline after the work has completed.
breakdown: Wait-Job avoids racing the background work.
Receive-Job emits the job's output into the current pipeline.
lessons.task: Run a job that returns background-ready, wait for it, receive that output, and remove the job.
hints: Pipe the captured job through Wait-Job and then Receive-Job before cleanup.

checks.description: The job's output was received.

lessons.completion: Receiving output and removing the job are separate operations; use -Keep when the same output must be read again.

lessons.title: Discover available modules
lessons.about: Get-Module inspects modules loaded in the session or installed on the module search path.
breakdown: -ListAvailable searches installed modules.
The name narrows the result to a built-in module.
lessons.task: Print the name of the installed Microsoft.PowerShell.Archive module.
hints: Use -ListAvailable, then select the first Name.

checks.description: The built-in utility module name was printed.

lessons.completion: Modules package commands and can be discovered before they are imported.

lessons.title: Load a built-in module
lessons.about: Import-Module loads commands from a module into the current PowerShell session; this rep allows only a built-in module.
breakdown: The module name resolves through PSModulePath.
-PassThru returns the loaded module object.
lessons.task: Import Microsoft.PowerShell.Archive and print its name.
hints: Use -PassThru, then expand Name.

checks.description: The imported built-in module name was printed.

lessons.completion: Import only trusted modules and review their source and scope before use.

lessons.title: Measure execution time
lessons.about: Measure-Command times a local expression and returns a TimeSpan describing its elapsed duration.
breakdown: The script block contains a static local expression.
The result is a TimeSpan object.
lessons.task: Measure the static expression 1 + 1 and print only elapsed ticks.
hints: Measure the expression, then expand Ticks.

checks.description: A non-negative tick count was printed.

lessons.completion: Measure-Command is useful for coarse comparisons; repeat measurements before drawing conclusions.

lessons.title: Create and format dates
lessons.about: Get-Date retrieves the current time or parses a supplied date into a DateTime object that can be formatted and compared.
breakdown: The supplied value makes the result deterministic.
-Format controls the output text.
lessons.task: Format the supplied date 2000-01-02 as yyyy-MM-dd.
hints: Use the exact custom date format.

checks.description: The deterministic date was formatted correctly.

lessons.completion: Keep DateTime objects structured until the final presentation or serialization step.

lessons.title: Calculate elapsed time
lessons.about: New-TimeSpan creates a TimeSpan from explicit endpoints or duration components.
breakdown: -Start supplies the first DateTime.
-End supplies the later DateTime.
lessons.task: Print the total days between 2026-01-01 and 2026-01-03.
hints: Expand the TotalDays property.

checks.description: The two-day interval was printed.

lessons.completion: TimeSpan properties make durations easier to compare than formatted strings.

lessons.title: Select a random input object
lessons.about: Get-Random returns random numbers or randomly selects objects supplied through -InputObject.
breakdown: -InputObject supplies the candidate collection.
One candidate is returned by default.
lessons.task: Select from an input collection containing only the number 7.
hints: A one-item input makes the result deterministic.

checks.description: The only candidate value was returned.

lessons.completion: Get-Random is convenient for sampling, but security-sensitive randomness needs threat-specific review.

lessons.title: Inspect regional settings
lessons.about: Get-Culture returns the current culture object used for formatting numbers, dates, currencies, and comparisons.
lessons.example_output:
LCID Name  DisplayName
---- ----  -----------
1033 en-US English (United States)
breakdown: Name is the culture identifier.
Other properties describe formatting conventions.
lessons.task: Print only the current culture name.
hints: Expand the Name property.

checks.description: The current culture name was printed.

lessons.completion: Culture affects parsing and formatting, so automation should make expectations explicit.

lessons.title: Inspect the PowerShell host
lessons.about: Get-Host returns information about the application hosting the PowerShell engine, including its version and capabilities.
breakdown: The host is separate from the operating system.
Version identifies the PowerShell host version.
lessons.task: Print the current host version as dotted text.
hints: Expand Version, then call its safe ToString member through ForEach-Object.

checks.description: A dotted PowerShell host version was printed.

lessons.completion: Host and engine versions help explain feature and behavior differences between environments.

lessons.title: Query CIM system information
lessons.about: Get-CimInstance queries Windows management data and returns structured CIM instances without screen scraping.
lessons.example_output:
SystemDirectory Organization BuildNumber RegisteredUser SerialNumber Version
...
breakdown: Win32_OperatingSystem names a CIM class.
The result exposes system properties as object members.
lessons.task: Print only the operating-system caption from CIM.
hints: Query the class, then expand Caption.

checks.description: A Windows operating-system caption was printed.

lessons.completion: CIM queries are a structured foundation for Windows inventory and diagnostics.

lessons.title: Collect broad computer information
lessons.about: Get-ComputerInfo aggregates operating-system, hardware, firmware, and configuration details into one large object.
breakdown: Get-ComputerInfo can be relatively expensive.
Select-Object narrows the broad object early.
lessons.task: Print only the Windows product name.
hints: Expand WindowsProductName from the result.

checks.description: A Windows product name was printed.

lessons.completion: Select only the properties you need from broad inventory commands.

lessons.title: List installed Windows updates
lessons.about: Get-HotFix reads installed update records and returns identifiers, descriptions, installation dates, and related metadata.
breakdown: The command is read-only.
The first record is sufficient for a short inventory rep.
lessons.task: Print the HotFixID of the first installed update record.
hints: Select the first record and expand HotFixID.

checks.description: A Windows update identifier was printed.

lessons.completion: Update inventory is one signal; support status and deployment policy require additional context.

lessons.title: Inspect physical disks
lessons.about: Get-Disk returns Windows disk objects with numbers, sizes, partition styles, health, and operational status.
lessons.example_output:
Number Friendly Name Serial Number HealthStatus OperationalStatus Total Size Partition Style
------ ------------- ------------- ------------ ----------------- ---------- ---------------
0      ...                         Healthy      Online            ...        GPT
breakdown: Disk numbers identify storage devices in management cmdlets.
This rep performs read-only inspection.
lessons.task: Print the number of the first disk Windows reports.
hints: Select the first disk and expand Number.

checks.description: A numeric disk identifier was printed.

lessons.completion: Disk operations can be destructive; begin with read-only inventory and verify identifiers carefully.

lessons.title: Inspect mounted volumes
lessons.about: Get-Volume returns volume objects with drive letters, labels, file systems, sizes, and health state.
lessons.example_output:
DriveLetter FriendlyName FileSystemType DriveType HealthStatus SizeRemaining Size
----------- ------------ -------------- --------- ------------ ------------- ----
C                        NTFS           Fixed     Healthy      ...           ...
breakdown: Volumes are distinct from physical disks.
DriveLetter can be null for unlettered volumes.
lessons.task: Print the first non-empty drive letter.
hints: Filter out null DriveLetter values before selecting the first.

checks.description: A drive letter was printed.

lessons.completion: Volumes expose file systems and capacity; disks represent underlying storage devices.

lessons.title: Inspect assigned IP addresses
lessons.about: Get-NetIPAddress returns structured address assignments across Windows network interfaces.
lessons.example_output:
IPAddress InterfaceIndex InterfaceAlias AddressFamily Type PrefixLength PrefixOrigin SuffixOrigin AddressState PolicyStore
...
breakdown: -AddressFamily narrows the query to IPv4.
Each result includes address and interface properties.
lessons.task: Print the first IPv4 address Windows reports.
hints: Filter by IPv4 and expand IPAddress.

checks.description: An IPv4 address was printed.

lessons.completion: Address objects retain interface, prefix, origin, and state information for later filtering.

lessons.title: Summarize interface configuration
lessons.about: Get-NetIPConfiguration summarizes adapters, IP addresses, gateways, and DNS servers as related objects.
lessons.example_output:
InterfaceAlias : Ethernet
InterfaceIndex : 4
IPv4Address    : 10.0.0.5
IPv4DefaultGateway : ...
DNSServer : ...
breakdown: Each object represents one interface configuration.
InterfaceAlias is a human-readable adapter name.
lessons.task: Print the alias of the first configured network interface.
hints: Select the first object and expand InterfaceAlias.

checks.description: A network interface alias was printed.

lessons.completion: Use the related address, gateway, and DNS properties instead of parsing ipconfig text.

lessons.title: Inspect network adapters
lessons.about: Get-NetAdapter returns physical and virtual network adapter objects with status, speed, names, and interface details.
lessons.example_output:
Name InterfaceDescription ifIndex Status MacAddress LinkSpeed
---- -------------------- ------- ------ ---------- ---------
Ethernet ...              4       Up     ...        10 Gbps
breakdown: Status identifies whether the adapter is operational.
Name is suitable for later adapter cmdlets.
lessons.task: Print the name of the first network adapter.
hints: Select the first adapter and expand Name.

checks.description: A network adapter name was printed.

lessons.completion: Adapter inventory is read-only here; changing adapters can disconnect a machine.

lessons.title: Inspect the routing table
lessons.about: Get-NetRoute returns Windows routing entries as objects with destinations, next hops, metrics, and interfaces.
lessons.example_output:
ifIndex DestinationPrefix NextHop RouteMetric ifMetric PolicyStore
------- ----------------- ------- ----------- -------- -----------
...
breakdown: -AddressFamily narrows the route set.
DestinationPrefix represents a routed network.
lessons.task: Print the first IPv4 destination prefix.
hints: Expand DestinationPrefix from the first IPv4 route.

checks.description: An IPv4 destination prefix was printed.

lessons.completion: Route objects can be filtered by interface, destination, and metric without parsing columns.

lessons.title: Inspect TCP endpoints
lessons.about: Get-NetTCPConnection returns local TCP listeners and connections with addresses, ports, state, and owning process identifiers.

LocalAddress LocalPort RemoteAddress RemotePort State OwningProcess
------------ --------- ------------- ---------- ----- -------------
0.0.0.0      135       0.0.0.0       0          Listen ...
breakdown: -State Listen narrows the collection.
OwningProcess can be correlated with Get-Process.
lessons.task: Print the state of the first listening TCP endpoint.
hints: Query listening endpoints and expand State.

checks.description: A listening endpoint reported Listen.

lessons.completion: Connection objects preserve ports, addresses, states, and owning process IDs for correlation.

lessons.title: Test loopback reachability
lessons.about: Test-Connection sends ICMP echo requests and returns response objects; this rep is restricted to the local loopback name.
lessons.example_output:
Source Destination IPV4Address IPV6Address Bytes Time(ms)
------ ----------- ----------- ----------- ----- --------
...    localhost   127.0.0.1               32    0
breakdown: localhost keeps traffic on this machine.
-Count 1 performs one short probe.

hints: Use localhost and -Count 1, then expand Address.

checks.description: The loopback response address was printed.

lessons.completion: A successful echo confirms only this narrow path, not application availability.

lessons.title: Resolve the local host name
lessons.about: Resolve-DnsName performs structured DNS queries; this offline rep is limited to the local host name.
lessons.example_output:
Name Type TTL Section IPAddress
---- ---- --- ------- ---------
localhost A   ... Answer 127.0.0.1
breakdown: localhost avoids an external DNS dependency.
Returned records expose names, types, and addresses.
lessons.task: Resolve localhost and print the first record's Name property.
hints: Resolve only localhost, then expand Name.

checks.description: The local host name was resolved.

lessons.completion: Structured DNS records are easier to filter by record type than nslookup display text.

lessons.title: Inspect script execution policy
lessons.about: Get-ExecutionPolicy reports the effective PowerShell script execution policy without changing it.
breakdown: The result is the effective policy name.
-List can show policy by scope.
lessons.task: Print the effective execution policy for this process.
hints: No parameters are needed for the effective policy.

checks.description: An execution policy name was printed.

lessons.completion: Execution policy is a safety feature, not a complete security boundary.

lessons.title: Inspect a script signature
lessons.about: Get-AuthenticodeSignature reports whether a Windows file has a valid Authenticode signature and exposes signer details.
lessons.example_output:
SignerCertificate Status    StatusMessage Path
----------------- ------    ------------- ----
                  NotSigned ...           script.ps1
breakdown: The synthetic script is intentionally unsigned.
Status is a structured enumeration value.
lessons.task: Print only the signature status of note.ps1.
hints: Expand the Status property.

checks.description: The unsigned script reported NotSigned.

lessons.completion: A valid signature identifies integrity and signer context; trust decisions still require policy.

lessons.title: Copy a local access-control descriptor
lessons.about: Set-Acl applies a security descriptor to a path; this rep copies one between synthetic files inside the disposable workspace.
breakdown: Get-Acl supplies the source security descriptor.
Set-Acl applies it only to the local target file.
lessons.task: Apply reference.txt's access-control descriptor to target.txt, then print acl-copied.
hints: Pipe the reference ACL directly into Set-Acl for the target.

checks.description: The local ACL copy was confirmed.
The target file content was not changed.

lessons.completion: ACL changes can remove access; always capture and review the intended descriptor first.

lessons.title: List local user accounts
lessons.about: Get-LocalUser returns local Windows account objects with names, enabled state, descriptions, and account metadata.
lessons.example_output:
Name Enabled Description
---- ------- -----------
Administrator False Built-in account...
breakdown: The command reads the local account database.
Account state remains a structured property.
lessons.task: Print the name of the first local user account.
hints: Select the first account and expand Name.

checks.description: A local user account name was printed.

lessons.completion: This rep inventories accounts only; creating or changing accounts is outside its boundary.

lessons.title: List local groups
lessons.about: Get-LocalGroup returns local Windows security group objects and their descriptions.
lessons.example_output:
Name Description
---- -----------
Administrators Administrators have complete and unrestricted access...
breakdown: The local group database is queried read-only.
Names can be passed to membership cmdlets.
lessons.task: Print the name of the first local security group.
hints: Select the first group and expand Name.

checks.description: A local group name was printed.

lessons.completion: Group inventory is read-only here; membership changes require deliberate authorization.

lessons.title: Inspect local group membership
lessons.about: Get-LocalGroupMember lists users and groups contained in a local Windows security group.
lessons.example_output:
ObjectClass Name                PrincipalSource
----------- ----                ---------------
User        HOST\LocalAdmin     Local
breakdown: S-1-5-32-544 identifies the built-in administrators group on every language of Windows.
ObjectClass distinguishes users from nested groups.
lessons.task: Resolve S-1-5-32-544, then print the object class of its first group member.
hints: Resolve the group by its invariant SID, then select the first member and expand ObjectClass.

checks.description: A group member object class was printed.

lessons.completion: Membership inspection is a key step before reviewing local privilege assignments.

lessons.title: Inspect scheduled tasks
lessons.about: Get-ScheduledTask returns registered Windows task definitions with names, paths, states, actions, triggers, and principals.
breakdown: The command reads Task Scheduler registrations.
TaskName and TaskPath identify each definition.
lessons.task: Print the name of the first registered scheduled task.
hints: Select the first task and expand TaskName.

checks.description: A scheduled task name was printed.

lessons.completion: This rep performs task inventory only and does not register, start, or remove tasks.

lessons.title: Query modern Windows event logs
lessons.about: Get-WinEvent queries classic and modern Windows event logs and returns structured event and log metadata objects.
lessons.example_output:
LogMode MaximumSizeInBytes RecordCount LogName
------- ------------------ ----------- -------
Circular ...               ...         Application
breakdown: -ListLog requests log metadata rather than event records.
Application is a standard local log.
lessons.task: Print the LogName for the local Application event log.
hints: Use -ListLog Application and expand LogName.

checks.description: The Application log name was printed.

lessons.completion: Get-WinEvent supports structured filtering that scales better than reading every event.

lessons.title: List classic event logs
lessons.about: Get-EventLog reads classic Windows event logs and remains useful on Windows PowerShell for legacy workflows.
lessons.example_output:
Max(K) Retain OverflowAction Entries Log
------ ------ -------------- ------- ---
...    ...    OverwriteOlder ...     Application
breakdown: -List returns classic log containers.
The Log property contains each log name.
lessons.task: Print the name of the first classic Windows event log.
hints: Use -List, then expand Log from the first result.

checks.description: A classic event log name was printed.

lessons.completion: Get-WinEvent is preferred for newer event channels and richer filtering.

lessons.title: Run a local script block
lessons.about: Invoke-Command can execute script blocks locally or through remoting; this rep permits only a static local arithmetic expression.

The script block contains only static arithmetic.
lessons.task: Use a local script block to calculate 2 + 3.
hints: Use -ScriptBlock with the static expression.

checks.description: The local expression returned five.

lessons.completion: Real remoting requires explicit authorization, trusted endpoints, authentication, and network controls.

lessons.title: Enable stricter script rules
lessons.about: Set-StrictMode makes common scripting mistakes fail earlier, including references to uninitialized variables and invalid properties.
breakdown: -Version Latest enables all current strict checks.
The setting affects only this disposable scope.
lessons.task: Enable the latest strict-mode rules for this PowerShell session, then print strict-mode-enabled.
hints: Use -Version Latest.

checks.description: The strict-mode step was confirmed.

lessons.completion: Strict mode catches many mistakes early and belongs near the start of reusable scripts.

lessons.title: Query legacy WMI data
lessons.about: Get-WmiObject queries Windows Management Instrumentation and appears in many existing Windows PowerShell scripts.
lessons.example_output:
SystemDirectory Organization BuildNumber RegisteredUser SerialNumber Version
...
breakdown: Win32_OperatingSystem names the WMI class.
The result exposes system properties as an object.
lessons.task: Print the operating-system caption from legacy WMI.
hints: Query the operating-system class and expand Caption.

checks.description: A Windows operating-system caption was printed.

lessons.completion: Prefer CIM cmdlets for new automation while recognizing WMI in established Windows PowerShell code.

lessons.title: Inspect the Windows time zone
lessons.about: Get-TimeZone returns the current Windows time-zone object with its identifier, display name, offset, and daylight rules.

Id : Pacific Standard Time
DisplayName : (UTC-08:00) Pacific Time...

Other properties describe offsets and daylight support.
lessons.task: Print only the current Windows time-zone identifier.
hints: Expand the Id property.

checks.description: The Windows time-zone identifier was printed.
